links.comparator_used: Unstructured nurse handover (control) vs ISBAR-structured nurse handover in a paired simulation
links.outcome: Hallucination frequency, escalation dialogue length, and safety-critical omissions
links.effect: Hallucinations 10.0% vs 26.5%; median 7 vs 9 turns; safety-critical omissions 16.0% vs 11.5% (ISBAR vs unstructured)
links.tradeoff: ISBAR did not reduce safety-critical omissions (16.0% with ISBAR vs 11.5% unstructured), so failure modes were not eliminated.
links.quote: Across 200 paired (n=400) escalation simulations, ISBAR-structured handover reduced hallucination frequency (10.0% vs 26.5%) and shortened esca lation dialogues (median 7 vs 9 turns) but did not reduce safety-critical omissions (16.0% vs 11.5%).

links.comparator_used: Independent review by experienced intensive care nurses on a subset of transcripts (human consensus)
links.outcome: Agreement between the automated rubric-based LLM evaluator and human assessment
links.effect: Agreement was limited across several domains. The automated evaluator had high sensitivity but low specificity for omission detection and differed systematically from humans on actionability and overall safety risk. Human reviewers themselves showed only moderate agreement for omission detection.
links.tradeoff: The automated evaluator may prioritize communication structure and fluency differently from clinicians assessing clinical completeness and safety, so expert oversight is still needed.
links.quote: Agreement between the automated evaluator and human consensus was limited across several domains, with the automated evaluator showing high sensitivity but low specificity for omission detection and systematically differing from human assessments of actionability and overall safety risk.
